title: An Indian Staffing CEO Forged H-1B Petitions for Years. Now the DOJ Is Revoking His Citizenship.
excerpt: Neeraj Sharma of New Jersey is one of 17 naturalized citizens targeted in the largest denaturalization sweep in American history. USCIS has been asked to supply 100 to 200 cases per month.
body:
Neeraj Sharma built a business on paperwork. As the owner and CEO of Magnavision LLC, an information technology staffing company in New Jersey, he filed H-1B visa petitions on behalf of workers he said would be employed at a major global financial institution. The petitions included letters on the institution's corporate letterhead, bearing the forged signatures of its executives.

There were eleven of them. Each one a fraud.

On June 8, the Department of Justice announced it had filed denaturalization actions against Sharma and 16 other naturalized U.S. citizens in what officials described as the largest single exercise of the government's denaturalization powers in American history. Sharma, 50 years old and a native of India, faces the revocation of the citizenship he obtained in December 2017 — a citizenship the government says he secured by lying under oath.

## The Fraud

The scheme was straightforward. Sharma filed H-1B petitions with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services claiming that the visa beneficiaries would work at a particular financial institution. To make the petitions appear legitimate, he fabricated letters on the institution's official letterhead and forged the signatures of its executives.

When Sharma applied for naturalization in 2017, he was asked — under penalty of perjury — whether he had ever committed a crime for which he was not arrested, whether he had given any U.S. government officials false or misleading information, and whether he had lied to gain immigration benefits. He answered no to all three questions.

He was subsequently convicted of fraud and misuse of visas under federal law, for offenses committed between April 2015 and April 2017 — a period that overlapped with his naturalization application.

## The Larger Sweep

Sharma's case is one of 17 denaturalization actions announced simultaneously, targeting individuals from 13 countries accused of offenses ranging from child sexual abuse to narcotics trafficking to financial fraud. The DOJ described the filing as an escalation of the Trump administration's denaturalization programme.

"American citizenship is a privilege, and it must be earned honestly," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. "If you come here, break our laws, and lie in your immigration proceedings, you forfeit that privilege."

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Department of Justice "maintains a zero-tolerance policy for the abuse of this process."

The numbers suggest this is not rhetoric. Between 1990 and 2017, the U.S. government averaged just 11 denaturalization cases per year. During Trump's first term, that rose to about 25 annually. Now, USCIS field offices have been instructed to supply the Office of Immigration Litigation with 100 to 200 denaturalization referrals per month throughout 2026.

That is an order-of-magnitude increase.

## What Denaturalization Means

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalized citizen's citizenship can be revoked if it was "illegally procured" or obtained through concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation. The process is civil, not criminal — the government must file suit in federal court and prove its case. The individual retains the right to a hearing.

If denaturalization succeeds, the individual loses their U.S. citizenship entirely. They revert to their previous immigration status — which, in many cases, means they become deportable.

The process is complex and has historically moved slowly through the courts. But the current administration has made it clear that it intends to use denaturalization as a routine enforcement tool, not an exceptional one.

## The Chilling Effect

For the estimated 23 million naturalized U.S. citizens — and the millions more in the pipeline — the expansion of denaturalization creates a climate of heightened scrutiny. Indian immigrants, who represent one of the largest groups of naturalized citizens and H-1B holders, are paying particularly close attention.

The Sharma case is especially uncomfortable because it involves the H-1B programme itself — the same system that has been the primary pathway for hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals to build careers and lives in the United States. Staffing company fraud, while perpetrated by a minority of actors, has been used to justify broader restrictions on the programme, including the now-struck-down $100,000 fee.

Immigration attorneys say the message is clear: misrepresentations on any immigration application, no matter how long ago, can now surface as grounds for losing citizenship. The statute of limitations for denaturalization does not exist — the government can bring a case at any time.

For the vast majority of Indian-Americans who obtained their citizenship honestly, the legal risk is minimal. But the political signal is unmistakable: the era of routine naturalisation as the final, irreversible step in the immigration journey may be over.
